title: Other options shot down ; Familes of those killed by police asking why cops' first reaction is to reach for their gun
article: Her mentally ill sister was gunned down by Toronto Police while brandishing a knife outside her home.

Lili Steer wants to know why another option wasn't used when police knew what awaited them from the 911 call: Why not try to reason with Sylvia Klibingaitis from behind a shield? Why not retreat to a safe distance so de-escalation methods could be attempted on the distraught 52-year-old grandmother?

But the police experts testifying at the inquest looking into the police shootings of Klibingaitis, as well as Reyal Jardine-Douglas, 25, and Michael Eligon, 29, maintained that reaching for their gun in such a situation is the officer's safest and best option.
Even if the person is in emotional distress.

Forget about shields and soft voice tones, batons and even Tasers, the three trainers from the Ontario Police College all agreed that when faced with a sharp-edged weapon, they instruct recruits to create distance and draw their firearm.
Klibingaitis' sister seemed stunned that no other alternatives appear to be acceptable to them. "It seems like we have no choice but to shoot," she said incredulously.
So why are we having this inquest at all?

The five-member jury is expected to hear eight weeks of testimony in the hope they will come up with recommendations to avert such fatal police shootings when responding to calls about the mentally ill. And there are a lot of them. Toronto Police received 20,000 calls in both 2011 and 2012 involving people believed to be either experiencing an emotional disturbance or suffering from a mental disorder.
But despite many such inquests and countless recommendations in the past, it seems the police college curriculum hasn't changed much at all: Mentally ill or not--reach for your gun.
Even the Taser--offered up by many proponents as the magic answer to deal with the emotionally disturbed-- is not the weapon of choice in a knife situation.

Trainer John Zeyen said Tasers aren't accurate enough and need to be deployed too closely to be safe for the police officer. "It would be rare" to use a stun gun in such knife-wielding scenarios, he told the inquest.

Zeyen does believe, however, that the high voltage electric shock is useful to subdue those with excited delirium-- a condition marked by aggressive and violent behaviour that is sometimes associated with severe mental illness.

But lawyer Peter Rosenthal, representing Eligon's family, questioned how that can be when the Taser manufacturer itself includes in its eight pages of warnings a caution that people suffering from excited delirium and severe agitation may be "particularly susceptible" to the effects of a stun gun and it "may cause or contribute to sudden death."
In fact, an inquest this summer in Midhurst concluded that a Taser was a contributing factor in the death of a 27-year-old schizophrenic with excited delirium.
Zeyen insisted that his research has shown the device to be "generally very safe to use."

Tasers are a hot button at this inquest. The weapon has been under intense scrutiny ever since Polish immigrant Robert Dziekanski died in 2007 after being Tasered several times by police at Vancouver's airport.

The Braidwood inquiry, which looked into Dziekanski's death, recommended that police be required to use "de-escalation and/or crisis intervention techniques" before deploying Tasers on emotionally disturbed people. The inquest heard there is no such requirement under Ontario's guidelines.

Right now, Tasers can only be used by tactical officers and road sergeants. In August, following public outrage over the police shooting of teen Sammy Yatim on an empty TTC streetcar, the Ontario government announced that individual police services can now decide whether they want to outfit their frontline officers with stun guns.

Are they the answer? From the evidence so far, it seems Tasers probably wouldn't have been used in any of the three cases now under review. And Klibingaitis, Jardine-Douglas and Eligon would still have died from a police bullet.
